                                                                                                           17B38, 20D08 (MSC2020)

                                                               Rota—Baxter operators on groups
                                                                   Valeriy G. Bardakov, Vsevolod Gubarev

                                                                                   Abstract
arXiv:2103.01848v2 [math.GR] 2 May 2021




                                                   Theory of Rota—Baxter operators on rings and algebras has been developed
                                               since 1960. Recently, L. Guo, H. Lang, Y. Sheng [arXiv:2009.03492] have deﬁned the
                                               notion of Rota—Baxter operator on a group. We provide some general constructions
                                               of Rota—Baxter operators on a group. Given a map on a group, we study its
                                               extensions to a Rota—Baxter operator. We state the connection between Rota—
                                               Baxter operators on a group and Rota—Baxter operators on an associated Lie ring.
                                               We describe Rota—Baxter operators on sporadic simple groups.
                                                   Keywords: Rota—Baxter operator, Rota—Baxter group, simple group, sporadic
                                               group, factorization.


                                          1    Introduction
                                              Rota—Baxter operators for commutative algebras ﬁrstly appear in the paper of
                                          G. Baxter [3] in 1960. Since that time the theory of Rota—Baxter operators has been
                                          developed by diﬀerent authors including J.-C. Rota, L. Guo, C. Bai, and K. Ebrahimi-
                                          Fard, see details in the monograph [13]. Maybe, the most important role of Rota—Baxter
                                          operators is their connections to Yang—Baxter equation [4, 21], Loday algebras [2, 12],
                                          double Poisson algebras [10, 20] and others.
                                              In September 2020 [14], L. Guo, H. Lang, Y. Sheng deﬁned the notion of Rota—Baxter
                                          operator (RB-operator, short) on a group. A map B : G → G is called a Rota—Baxter
                                          operator (of weight 1) if B(g)B(h) = B(gB(g)hB(g)−1) for all g, h ∈ G. A group G with
                                          a Rota—Baxter operator B is called a Rota—Baxter group.
                                              The main motivation of [14] to introduce this new notion is following. Given a Rota—
                                          Baxter Lie group (G, B), then the tangent map of B at the identity is a Rota—Baxter
                                          operator of weight 1 on the Lie algebra of the Lie group G. If a crossed homomorphism φ
                                          from a group G to itself is invertible, then φ−1 is an RB-operator on G [14]. Some basic
                                          examples and properties of Rota—Baxter groups were also stated in the pioneer work [14].
                                              In November 2020 [9], M. Goncharov introduced the notion of a Rota—Baxter operator
                                          on a cocommutative Hopf algebra as a combination of both Rota—Baxter operators on
                                          a group and on a Lie algebra. In particular, every such Rota—Baxter operator on the
                                          Hopf algebra k[G] arises as a linear extension of an RB-operator deﬁned on a group G.
                                              The main goal of the current work is to give diﬀerent constructions of Rota—Baxter
                                          operators on a group. We provide constructions via factorizations, homomorphisms,
                                          projections, direct products, and ones deﬁned by exact formulas (see §4–6). In particular,
                                          we state in Proposition 5.1 that any homomorphism from a group to its abelian subgroup
                                          is a Rota—Baxter operator. In [1, 5, 11], RB-operators on kn , a sum of n copies of a ﬁeld k
                                          considered as a commutative k-algebra, were studied. In Theorem 6.3 we construct by
                                          an RB-operator R on kn an RB-operator B on Gn = G × G × . . . × G for a given group G.


                                                                                       1
    We study extensions of maps on a given group to an RB-operator and extensions
of Rota—Baxter groups (see §7–8). We ﬁnd the necessary (Lemma 7.5) and suﬃcient
conditions (Theorem 7.7) under which a map β on a group G can be extended to an
RB-operator on G.
    Let G be a group, it is well-known
                                    L that by its lower central series Gn , n = 1, 2, . . .,
one can associate Lie ring L(G) = n≥1 Gn /Gn+1. We prove that by any RB-operator B
on G such that B(Gn ) ⊂ Gn for all n ≥ 1, we may deﬁne the RB-operator of weight 1
on L(G) (Proposition 9.1).
    It is natural to ask about complete description of RB-operators on a given group G.
Naturally, one should do such classiﬁcation up to action of automorphisms of G (see
Lemma 2.9) and up to involution ˜ (see Lemma 2.8). We make the following step in
the direction of classiﬁcation of RB-operators on ﬁnite simple groups: we describe RB-
operators on all sporadic simple groups.
    Let us give short outline of the work. In §2, we give required preliminaries on
Rota—Baxter operators on groups. In §3, we consider the induced on a group G by an
RB-operator B new group product g ◦ h = gB(g)hB(g)−1. The group GB = hG, ◦i was
deﬁned in [14].
    In §4, we study constructions of RB-operators appeared due to exact factorizations
(double and triple) of groups and properties of such constructions.
    In §5, we give constructions of RB-operators involved homomorphisms, projections
and some exact formulas. We ﬁnd RB-operators on n-abelian groups (Proposition 5.2)
and on 2-step nilpotent groups (Corollary 5.5). In §6, we study RB-operators on direct
products of groups.
    In §7, we study extensions of a given map β on a group G to an RB-operator B on G.
Applying the necessary condition, we construct and study the auxiliary group Ḡβ . In §8,
the problems concerning extensions of Rota—Baxter groups are posted.
    In §9, we ﬁnd a connection between RB-operators on a group and RB-operators on
its associated Lie ring.
    In §10, we state that on a simple group G without ﬁxed-point-free automorphisms
every Rota—Baxter operator with trivial kernel has the form B(g) = g −1 (Theorem 10.1).
Applying this result and the list of all factorizations of sporadic groups [8], we describe
all RB-operators on all sporadic simple groups in Theorem 10.4.


2    Preliminaries
   Let A be an algebra over a ﬁeld k. A linear operator R on A is called a Rota—Baxter
operator of weight λ ∈ k if

                         R(x)R(y) = R(R(x)y + xR(y) + λxy).                            (2.1)

for all x, y ∈ A. An algebra endowed with a Rota—Baxter operator is called a Rota—
Baxter algebra.
    Let us consider an analogue of Rota—Baxter operator of weights ±1 on a group.



                                             2
Definition 2.1 ([14]). Let G be a group.
  a) A map B : G → G is called a Rota—Baxter operator of weight 1 if

                            B(g)B(h) = B(gB(g)hB(g)−1)                              (2.2)

for all g, h ∈ G.
    b) A map C : G → G is called a Rota—Baxter operator of weight −1 if

                             C(g)C(h) = C(C(g)hC(g)−1g)

for all g, h ∈ G.

   A group endowed with a Rota—Baxter operator is called a Rota—Baxter group (RB-
group).

Lemma 2.2. If C : G → G is a Rota—Baxter operator of weight −1 on a group G, then
             e
the operator C(g) = gC(g −1), g ∈ G, is also a Rota—Baxter operator of weight −1.

   In [14] it was proved that if B is a Rota—Baxter operator of weight 1 on a group G,
then the map C(g) = B(g −1 ) is an Rota—Baxter operator of weight −1. Another con-
nection between Rota—Baxter operators of weights 1 and −1 gives

Proposition 2.3. If B : G → G is Rota—Baxter operator of weight 1 on a group G, then
the operator C(g) = gB(g), g ∈ G, is a Rota—Baxter operator of weight −1 on G.

Proof. One needs to check (2.2). By the deﬁnition of C it is equivalent to

                           gB(g)hB(h) = C(gB(g)hB(g)−1),

i. e.,
                          B(g)B(h) = B(gB(g)hB(g)−1).
   Hence, we have a bijection between Rota—Baxter operators of weight 1 and −1 on
a group G. To the end of the paper we will consider only Rota—Baxter operators of
weight 1 and will call them simply Rota—Baxter operators (RB-operators).

Example 2.4. Let G be a group. Then
  a) the map B0 (g) = e is an RB-operator on G,
  b) the map B−1 (g) = g −1 is an RB-operator on G.

    We will call the Rota—Baxter operators B0 and B−1 as elementary RB-operators.
A group G is called RB-elementary, if any RB-operator on G is elementary. It is evident
that every cyclic group of prime order is elementary. Other examples of elementary
groups will be given in the last section.
    Given a group G, we use the usual notation of the commutator [g, h] = g −1 h−1 gh for
g, h ∈ G; the commutator subgroup [H, L] for subgroups H, L of G is a subgroup that is
generated by the set of commutators {[h, l] | h ∈ H, l ∈ L}.
    Let us state some elementary facts about RB-operators.


                                           3
Lemma 2.5. If B : G → G is a Rota—Baxter operator on a group G, then
  a) B(e) = e;
  b) B(g)B(g −1) = B([g −1, B(g)−1 ]);
  c) B(g)B(B(g)) = B(gB(g));
  d) B(g)−1 = B(B(g)−1 g −1 B(g)) for any g ∈ G.

Proof. a) It follows from (2.2) considered with g = h = e.
   b) It follows from (2.2) considered with h = g −1 .
   c) It follows from (2.2) considered with h = B(g).
   d) It follows from the equalities

 B(g)B(B(g)−1g −1B(g))=B(gB(g)B(g)−1g −1 B(g)B(g)−1)=B(gg −1) = B(e) = e. (2.3)

Lemma is proved.
    In [14] it was noted (without proof) that given a group G and a Rota—Baxter oper-
ator B on G the sets ker B and Im B are subgroups of G. Let us write down the proof
for convenience.

Lemma 2.6 ([14]). Let B be a Rota—Baxter operator on a group G. Then
  a) ker B is a subgroup of G,
  b) Im B is a subgroup of G.

Proof. a) We have B(e) = e by Lemma 2.5a. Let g, h ∈ ker B, then by (2.2)

               B(g −1 ) = B(g)B(g −1) = B(gB(g)g −1B(g)−1) = B(e) = e,
                      e = B(g)B(h) = B(gB(g)hB(g)−1) = B(gh).

   b) Directly by (2.2) we have that if g, h ∈ Im B, then gh ∈ Im B. Suppose that
g ∈ Im B, then g −1 ∈ Im B by Lemma 2.5d.
   When a Rota—Baxter operator B on a group G is invertible, i. e., the map B −1 : G →
G exists, then B −1 is a crossed homomorphism from G to itself [14]. The following result
can be useful in attempt to construct RB-operators B on a given group with ker B 6= {e}.

Lemma 2.7. Let B be a Rota—Baxter operator on a group G. If B(g) = e for some
g ∈ G, then B(h) = B(gh) for any h ∈ G. In particular, if
                                      a
                                 G=      ker(B)gi
                                         i∈I

is the decomposition of G in the disjoint union of cosets, then B(x) = B(y) if x and y lie
in the same coset.

Proof. It follows from (2.2) considered with such g and h.
   The following claim gives a possibility to construct new RB-operators from the known
ones.

    In particular, B
    The following observation is very important when one is interested on the classiﬁcation
of all RB-operators on a given group.

Lemma 2.9. Let B be a Rota—Baxter operator on a group G. Let ϕ be an automorphism
of G. Then B (ϕ) = ϕ−1 Bϕ is a Rota—Baxter operator on a group G.

Proof. The following equalities imply the statement,

    ϕ(B (ϕ) (g)B (ϕ) (h)) = ϕ(ϕ−1 (B(ϕ(g)))ϕ−1(B(ϕ(h)))) = B(ϕ(g))B(ϕ(h))
       = B(ϕ(g)B(ϕ(g))ϕ(h)B(ϕ(g))−1) = ϕϕ−1 Bϕ(gϕ−1B(ϕ(g))hϕ−1 (B(ϕ(g))−1))
                                                   = ϕ(B (ϕ) (gB (ϕ) (g)h(B (ϕ) (g))−1 )).

   Thus, we may describe Rota—Baxter operators on a group up to conjugation with its
automorphism.

Lemma 2.10. Let G be a group, let ϕ be an automorphism ϕ of G and let B be
a Rota—Baxter operator on G. Then (B)      g
                                   e (ϕ) = B (ϕ) .


Proof. We have

 e (ϕ) (g) = ϕ−1 (B(ϕ(g))))
(B)               e                                                            g
                            = ϕ−1 ((ϕ(g))−1B((ϕ(g))−1)) = g −1 B (ϕ) (g −1 ) = B (ϕ) (g).


    Let (G, B) and (G′ , B ′ ) be Rota—Baxter groups. A map Φ : G → G′ is a Rota—Baxter
group homomorphism if Φ is a group homomorphism such that ΦB = B ′ Φ.
    A group G is called factorizable if G = HL for some its subgroups H and L. The
expression G = HL is called a factorization of G. If additionally H ∩ L = {e}, then such
factorization is called exact. If H and L are proper subgroups of G, we call a factorization
G = HL as a proper one.


3      Rota—Baxter induced group
     In [14] a new binary operation ◦ : G → G on a Rota—Baxter group (G, B) was deﬁned.

Proposition 3.1 ([14]). Let (G, ·, B) be a Rota—Baxter group.
  a) The pair (G, ◦) with the product

                                  g ◦ h = gB(g)hB(g)−1,                                      (3.1)

where g, h ∈ G, is also a group.
   b) The operator B is a Rota—Baxter operator on the group (G, ◦).
   c) The map B : (G, ◦) → (G, ·) is a homomorphism of Rota—Baxter groups.


                                              5
   We will denote the group (G, ◦) as GB .
   Given a group G and a Rota—Baxter operator B on G, consider a map B+ on G
deﬁned as follows, B+ (g) = gB(g) [14]. Note that B+ is a group homomorphism from
GB to G. Lemma 2.5c says that B+ B = BB+ .

Example 3.2. Let G be a group with a Rota—Baxter operator B.
  a) If B = B0 , then
                         g ◦ h = gB0 (g)hB0 (g)−1 = gh.
Hence, both products ◦ and · coincide.
   b) If B = B−1 , then

                                 g ◦ h = gB−1 (g)hB−1 (g)−1 = hg.

Hence, (G, ◦) is a group with the opposite product.
   c) If G is abelian, then g ◦ h = g · h for all g, h ∈ G.

    In [14], L. Guo, H. Lang, and Yu. Sheng proved the results analogous to the ones
stated by M.A. Semenov-Tyan-Shanskii for Lie algebras [21].

Proposition 3.3 ([14]). If (G, B) is an RB-group, then
  a) ker(B) and ker(B+ ) are normal in GB ;
  b) ker(B) ✂ Im (B+ ) and ker(B+ ) ✂ Im (B) in G;
  c) We have the isomorphism of quotient groups

                              Im (B+ )/ ker(B) ∼
                                               = Im (B)/ ker(B+ );                                   (3.2)

   d) We have the factorization

                                        G = Im (B+ )Im (B).                                          (3.3)

   Let us ﬁnd the exact formulas for words written in terms of the operation ◦ in GB .
Given an integer k, denote by a◦(k) the kth power of a under the product ◦.

Proposition 3.4. Let (G, B) be a Rota—Baxter group. If A is a subset of G and
                              ◦(k )    ◦(k )            ◦(k )
                       w = ai1 1 ◦ ai2 2 ◦ . . . ◦ ais s ,      aij ∈ A, kj ∈ Z,

is presented by a word under the operation ◦, then

 w=(ai1 B(ai1 ))k1 (ai2 B(ai2 ))k2 . . . (ais B(ais ))ks B(ais )−ks B(ais−1 )−ks−1 . . . B(ai1 )−k1 . (3.4)

In particular, a◦(k) = (B+ (a))k (B(a))−k for every integer k and a◦(−1) = B(a)−1 a−1 B(a).

Proof. Firstly, it is easy to show by induction on n ∈ N that a◦(n) = (B+ (a))n (B(a))−n .
Indeed, for n = 0 we have e = e. The induction step follows from the equalities

               a◦(n) = a ◦ (a◦(n−1) ) = aB(a)a◦(n−1) B(a)−1 = (aB(a))n B(a)−n .


                                                    6
One can check directly that B(a)−1 a−1 B(a) is the inverse element to a in the group GB .
Now, again by induction on n ∈ N and by Lemma 2.5d we compute

    a◦(−n) = a◦(−1) ◦ (a◦(−(n−1)) )
     = B(a)−1 a−1 B(a)B(B(a)−1 a−1 B(a))(aB(a))−(n−1) B(a)n−1 (B(B(a)−1 a−1 B(a)))−1
                               = (aB(a))−1 (aB(a))−(n−1) B(a)n−1 B(a)1 = (aB(a))−n B(a)n .
                     ◦(k )            ◦(k )
   Denote w ′ = ai2 2 ◦ . . . ◦ ais s . Applying that B is a homomorphism from GB to G,
we get
        ◦(k )                                   ◦(k )        ◦(k )
w = ai1 1 ◦w ′ = (B+ (ai1 ))k1 (B(ai1 ))−k1 B(ai1 1 )w ′ B(ai1 1 )−1 = (B+ (ai1 ))k1 w ′(B(ai1 ))−k1 .

Thus, by induction on s we derive the formula (3.4).


4      Constructions via factorizations
     The next example allows us to construct non-elementary RB-operators.

Example 4.1 ([14]). Let G be a group. Given an exact factorization G = HL, a map
B : G → G deﬁned as follows,
                                  B(hl) = l−1
is a Rota—Baxter operator on G.

   Let us call such Rota—Baxter operator on G as a splitting Rota—Baxter operator.
Note that in this case GB ∼
                          = H × L and B+ (hl) = h.
Proposition 4.2. Let G be a group and let B : G → G be an RB-operator on G. Then
B is a splitting Rota—Baxter operator on G if and only if B(gB(g)) = e for all g ∈ G.

Proof. Suppose that B is a splitting RB-operator on G with subgroups H and L. Take
g = hl, where h ∈ H and l ∈ L. Then

                        B(gB(g)) = B(hlB(hl)) = B(hll−1 ) = B(h) = e.

   Conversely, suppose that B(gB(g)) = e for all g ∈ G. Let us prove that G =
ker(B)Im (B) and this factorization is exact. Firstly, let a ∈ ker(B) ∩ Im (B). Then
B(a) = e and there exists g ∈ G such that a = B(g). By the assumption, we have e =
B(gB(g)) = B(ga). Since ga, a ∈ ker(B), by Lemma 2.6a we conclude that g ∈ ker(B).
So, a = e.
   Secondly, let g ∈ G. The equality B(gB(g)) = e implies that gB(g) = a ∈ ker(B).
Thus, g = ab, where b = B(g)−1 ∈ Im (B) by Lemma 2.6b.

Remark 4.3. By Lemma 2.5, the condition B(gB(g)) = e is equivalent to the relation
B(g)B 2(g) = e or B 2 (g) = B(g)−1. It means that if B is a splitting RB-operator, then
B inverts all elements of Im (B).

                                                 7
   Let us extend Example 4.1 on some triple factorizations.
Proposition 4.4. Let G be a group such that G = HLM, where H, L, and M are
subgroups of G with pairwise trivial intersection. Let C be a Rota—Baxter operator
on L. Moreover, [H, L] = [C(L), M] = e. Then the map B : G → G deﬁned by the
formula
                                B(hlm) = C(l)m−1
is a Rota—Baxter operator on G.
Proof. Let h, h′ ∈ H, l, l′ ∈ L, and m, m′ ∈ M. Then

  C(l)C(l′ )m−1 m′−1 = C(l)m−1 C(l′ )m′−1 = B(hlm)B(h′ l′ m′ )
            = B(hlmB(hlm)h′ l′ m′ B(hlm)−1 ) = B(hlmC(l)m−1 h′ l′ m′ mC(l)−1 )
               = B(hlC(l)mm−1 h′ l′ C(l)−1 m′ m) = B(hh′ lC(l)l′ C(l)−1 m′ m)
                                                          = C(lC(l)l′ C(l)−1 )m−1 m′−1 ,
which is fulﬁlled by (2.2).
    Let us call a Rota—Baxter operator on G = HLM deﬁned by Proposition 4.4 with
the help of C as a triangular-splitting one. Note that GB ∼
                                                          = H × LC × M op , where M op
is the set M with the opposite product m ∗ m′ = m′ m.
Corollary 4.5. Let G = ha, bi be two generated 2-step nilpotent group. Put c = [b, a].
Then G = haihcihbi and for any integer k the map
                              B(aα cβ bγ ) = ckβ b−γ ,   α, β, γ ∈ Z,
is an RB-operator on G.
   Given a splitting RB-operator B on a group G, we have an exact factorization
                                       G = ker(B)Im (B).                                   (4.1)
It is easy to see that if G is abelian, then there exists a non-splitting RB-operator B on G
such that (4.1) is fulﬁlled. Indeed, if G is a direct sum of abelian subgroups: G = H × L,
then any map hl 7→ ϕ(l), where ϕ is an endomorphism of L, deﬁnes an RB-operator on G
satisfying (4.1).
     The next claim generalizes this observation.
Proposition 4.6. Given a semidirect product G = H ⋊ L, let C be a Rota—Baxter
operator on L. Then a map B : G → G deﬁned by the formula B(hl) = C(l), where
h ∈ H and l ∈ L, is a Rota—Baxter operator.
Proof. We state the claim by the following computations for h, h′ ∈ H and l, l′ ∈ L,
                                   B(hl)B(h′ l′ ) = C(l)C(l′ ),
                                                                  −1 −1
  B(hlB(hl)h′ l′ B(hl)−1 ) = B(hlC(l)h′ l′ C(l)−1 ) = B(hh′C(l) l lC(l)l′ C(l)−1 )
                                                      = C(lC(l)l′ C(l)−1 ) = C(l)C(l′ ).
   Note that GB ∼
                = H ⋊ LC .

                                                 8
5    Constructions via homomorphisms, projections, and
     exact formulas
   When G is an abelian group, then B is a Rota—Baxter operator on G if and only if
B is an endomorphism of G.

Proposition 5.1. a) Let (G, B) be a Rota—Baxter group and B be an automorphism
of G. Then G is abelian.
   b) If G a group and H is its abelian subgroup, then any homomorphism (or antiho-
momorphism) B : G → H is a Rota—Baxter operator.

Proof. Suppose that a Rota—Baxter operator B : G → G is an endomorphism, then

        B(g)B(h) = B(gB(g)hB(g)−1) = B(g)B 2 (g)B(h)(B 2 (g))−1,                    g, h ∈ G.

It is equivalent to the relation
                                        [B 2 (g), B(h)] = e.                                     (5.1)
Hence, b) is true. The proof for the case when B is an antihomomorphism from G to H
is analogous.
    If further B is an automorphism, then G is an abelian group by (5.1).
   The following several constructions of Rota—Baxter operators work only for groups
very close to abelian ones.
   Given an integer k, a group G is called k-abelian [18] if (gh)k = g k hk for all g, h ∈ G.

Proposition 5.2. Let G be a group, and ﬁx a natural n. A map B : G → G deﬁned as
follows B(g) = g n is a Rota—Baxter operator on G if and only if G is (n + 1)-abelian.

Proof. Given g, h ∈ G, the identity (2.2) for the map B(x) = xn has the form

         g n hn = (g n+1hg −n )n = g n+1hg −n g n+1 hg −n g n+1 . . . hg −n = g n (gh)n g −n .

So, it is equivalent to the equality (gh)n = hn g n or to the following one:

                                (hg)n+1 = h(gh)n g = hn+1 g n+1.

It means that B is a Rota—Baxter operator on G if and only if G is (n + 1)-abelian.
   Since every k-abelian group is also (1−k)-abelian group, we may represent the induced
product in GB as follows

                  g ◦ h = gg nhg −n = g n+1hn+1 h−n g −n = (gh)n+1(hg)−n .

Remark 5.3. The statement of Proposition 5.2 in “if” direction follows from Proposi-
tion 5.1, since the nth power of a (n + 1)-abelian group G lies in Z(G) [15].

Proposition 5.4. Let G be a group. Then a map B(x) = g −1x−1 g is a Rota—Baxter
operator on G if and only if [g, G] ⊂ Z(G).

                                                  9
Proof. Suppose that B(x) = g −1 x−1 g is a Rota—Baxter operator on G. It means that

          g −1x−1 y −1 g = g −1 (xg −1 x−1 gyg −1xg)−1 g = g −1 g −1x−1 gy −1g −1xgx−1 g

for all x, y ∈ G. This equality is equivalent to the following one,

                                x−1 y −1 = [g, x]x−1 y −1[g, x−1 ].

Denote s = x−1 y −1, then we have [x, g]s = [g, x−1 ] for all x, s ∈ G. Fixing x ∈ G, we
conclude that [g, x] ∈ Z(G) for every x ∈ G.
   Conversely, suppose that g ∈ G such an element that [g, x] ∈ Z(G) for every x ∈ G.
By the previous part, it is enough to state that [x, g] = [g, x−1 ] for all x, s ∈ G. Since

             [g, x−1 ] = g −1 xgx−1 = x−1 g −1 xg[g −1xg, x−1 ] = [x, g] · [xg , x−1 ],

we have to prove that [xg , x−1 ] = e. Denote c = [g, x−1 ]. We get it by the formulas

             [xg , x−1 ] = [[g, x−1 ]x, x−1 ] = [cx, x−1 ] = x−1 c−1 xcxx−1 = e.

   Given a group G with an element g such that [g, G] ⊂ Z(G), we may compute the
product of GB , where B(x) = g −1 x−1 g:

          x ◦ y = xB(x)yB(x)−1 = xg −1 x−1 gyg −1xg = yxg −1 x−1 gg −1xg = yx,

so this product coincides with the product induced by the RB-operator B−1 .
Corollary 5.5. Let G be a 2-step nilpotent group, g ∈ G, then the map Bg (x) = g −1 x−1 g
is a Rota—Baxter operator.
   It is evident that this map Bg is a bijection. Denote by RB(G) the set of all Rota—
Baxter operators on G. Hence, we have a map ϕ : G/[G, G] → RB(G) deﬁned as follows,
ϕ(g) = Bg .
   Let us try to construct a Rota—Baxter operator by the formula B(g) = agb with the
help of some ﬁxed a and b. In comparison to Proposition 5.4 we allow a and b be not
necessary inverse to each other, however we do not inverse g.
Corollary 5.6. Let G be a group, and ﬁx a, b ∈ G. A map B : G → G deﬁned as follows
B(g) = agb, is a Rota—Baxter operator on G if and only if G is abelian and b = a−1 ,
i. e., B = id.
Proof. If G is abelian, then every endomorphism of G is a Rota—Baxter operator on G,
including the identity map.
    Conversely, suppose that a map B on G deﬁned by the formula B(g) = agb is a Rota—
Baxter operator on G. Since B(e) = e, we have b = a−1 . Thus, B is an automorphism
of G and by Proposition 5.1a we have that G is abelian, and so B = id.
Definition 5.7. A Rota—Baxter group (G, B) has the deep m (m is a natural number
or ω) if it is a minimal such that

                     G > B(G) > B 2 (G) > · · · > B m (G) = B m+1 (G).

                                                10
   Note that the RB-group (G, B−1 ) has deep 0 and the RB-group (G, B), where |G| > 1,
B = B0 or B is splitting, has deep 1.
   The following example shows that there are RB-groups of inﬁnite deep.
Example 5.8. Let (Z, +) be the inﬁnite cycle group and B : Z → Z, B(x) = 2x for any
x ∈ Z. Then (Z, B) is a Rota—Baxter group and it has the deep ω since
                                                                   \
                                                                   ∞
                                    2                      ω
             Z > B(Z) = 2Z > B (Z) = 4Z > · · · > B (Z) =                B k (Z) = 0.
                                                                   k=1

    If Fn = hx1 , x2 , . . . , xn i is a free non-abelian group, then we can deﬁne its projection
π1 : Fn → hx1 i by
                                    π1 (x1 ) = x1 , π1 (xi ) = e, i 6= 1.
Then Fn = ker(π1 )hx1 i and for any integer k the map B(g) = π1 (g)k is a Rota—Baxter
operator on Fn . The following proposition generalizes this observation.
Proposition 5.9. Let G = K ∗ L be a free product with abelian L and π1 : G → L
be a projection on the second component. Then for any endomorphism χ of L the map
B(g) = χ(π1 (g)) is a Rota—Baxter operator on G.
Question 5.10. Let G be a group and H be its a proper subgroup. Under which
conditions there is a Rota—Baxter operator B such that B(G) = H? In particular, if
F is a free non-abelian group, is there an RB-operator on F such that its image is the
commutator subgroup F ′ of F ?


6    Constructions via direct products
    Using RB-operators on some groups, we can deﬁne RB-operators on direct products
of these groups, it follows from
Proposition 6.1. Let G be a group such that G = H × L.
   a) Let BH be a Rota—Baxter operator on H and let BL be a Rota—Baxter operator
on L. Then a map B : G → G deﬁned by the formula B(hl) = BH (h)BL (l), where h ∈ H
and l ∈ L, is a Rota—Baxter operator.
   b) If L is abelian and |L| > 2, then there exists a non-splitting Rota—Baxter operator
on G.
Proof. a) Straightforward.
    b) On the contrary, suppose that every Rota—Baxter operator on G is splitting.
Deﬁne a Rota—Baxter operator B(ψ) on G with the help of an automorphism ψ of L as
follows, B(ψ)((h, l)) = ψ(l), by Proposition 5.1 it is a Rota—Baxter operator on G. By
Proposition 4.2, we should have B(lB(l)) = ψ(l)ψ 2 (l) = e for all l ∈ L. Take ψ = id,
so we have l2 = e for all l ∈ L. Since L is abelian, we get that L is a direct sum of
copies of Z2 . By the condition |L| > 2, so we may ﬁnd nonzero and diﬀerent l1 , l2 ∈ L.
Let us consider an automorphism ψ of L which interchanges l1 and l2 and does not
change all other elements. It is easy to see that B(ψ) is non-splitting. We arrive at
a contradiction.

                                               11
   It is easy to check that the following example gives Rota—Baxter operators on Gn ,
below we will generalize it.
Example 6.2. Let Gn = G × G × . . . × G. Then the following maps from Gn to Gn

                      B((g1 , . . . , gn )) = (e, g1 , g2 g1 , g3 g2 g1 , . . . , gn−1gn−2 . . . g1 ),
               e 1 , . . . , gn )) = (g −1 , g −1g −1, g −1 g −1g −1 , . . . , g −1g −1 g −1 . . . g −1)
               B((g                    1      2   1     3    2   1              n   n−1 n−2         1

are Rota—Baxter operators.
    These Rota—Baxter operators may be extended to the ones on the inﬁnite Cartesian
product of G.
    Let R be a Rota—Baxter operator of weight 1 on the direct sum of ﬁelds (considered
as associative algebra) kn = ke1 ⊕ ke2 ⊕ . . . ⊕ ken , where ei ej = δij ei . A linear operator
         Pn
R(ei ) =    rik ek , rik ∈ k, is an RB-operator of weight 1 on kn if and only if the following
           k=1
conditions are satisﬁed [1, 5]:
   (1) rii = 0 and rik ∈ {0, 1} or rii = −1 and rik ∈ {0, −1} for all k 6= i;
   (2) if rik = rki = 0 for i 6= k, then ril rkl = 0 for all l 6∈ {i, k};
   (3) if rik 6= 0 for i 6= k, then rki = 0 and rkl = 0 or ril = rik for all l 6∈ {i, k}.
   Moreover, we may suppose that the matrix of R is upper-triangular [5, 11].

Corollary 6.5. We may slightly modify (6.1) as follows. Let ψ2 , . . . , ψn ∈ Aut(G). Then
a map P : Gn → Gn deﬁned by the formula

by (6.1). Note that P = B (ϕ) .
Corollary 6.6. Given a group G = H × H × L for some L and a non-trivial group H,
the map B : G → G deﬁned as follows, B((h1 , h2 , l)) = (e, h1 , e) is a non-splitting Rota—
Baxter operator.
Proof. Applying Example 6.2 and Proposition 5.1, we conclude that B is a Rota—Baxter
operator on G. Denote g = (h1 , h2 , l). Since B(gB(g)) = (e, h1 , eL ) is not the identity
of G when h1 6= e, the operator B is not splitting by Proposition 4.2.


7        Extensions of maps to RB-operators
   In the previous sections we have considered some possibilities to construct RB-
operators on groups. In general case we formulate
Question 7.1. Let G = hAi be a group generated by a set A = {ai | i ∈ I}. Suppose that
U = {ui }i∈I is a subset of G with the same cardinality as A. Under which conditions
the map β : A → U, ai 7→ ui , i ∈ I, can be (uniquely) extended to an RB-operator
B : G → G?

                                                                      13
   Suppose at ﬁrst that we know that (G, B) is an RB-group. What is a minimal subset
M ⊆ G such that the values B(m) for all m ∈ M uniquely deﬁne the values B(g) for all
elements of G?
   The next theorem gives the answer on this question.

Theorem 7.2. Let G be a group, let A = {ai }i∈I be some its subset, and let B an
RB-operator on G.
   a) We can ﬁnd the values of B on all elements of the subgroup hAiB ≤ (G, ◦) by the
values B(ai ), ai ∈ A. The image B(hAiB ) is generated by elements B(ai ), i ∈ G.
   b) If A is a generating set of GB , then the values B on A uniquely deﬁne the values
of B on all elements of G.
Proof. a) By assumption (G, B) is a Rota—Baxter group and B(ai ) = ui , i ∈ I. Suppose
that an element g of hAiB is presented by some word
                                ◦(k )     ◦(k )            ◦(k )
                       w = ai1 1 ◦ ai2 2 ◦ . . . ◦ ais s ,           aij ∈ A, kij ∈ Z.

Since B is a homomorphism from GB to G, we conclude that
                          ◦(k )  ◦(k )        ◦(k ) 
                B(w) = B ai1 1 B ai2 2 . . . B ais s = uki11 uki22 . . . ukiss .

Hence, we can ﬁnd the values of B on the group that is generated by the set A under the
product ◦.
   b) If the set hAiB is equal G, then we can ﬁnd all values B(g), g ∈ G by the values
B(ai ), ai ∈ A.
    Now we consider a question on construction of RB-operators on an arbitrary group G.
In this case we do not know generating set of GB , anyway we can take a generating set
of G and deﬁne a map β on this set. Let G = hAi be a group generated by a set
A = {ai | i ∈ I}. Suppose that U = {ui }i∈I is a subset of G with the same cardinality
as A and the map β : A → U is deﬁned by β(ai ) = ui , i ∈ I.
    Let us construct a group Ḡβ . To do this, we take a set of letters Ā = {āi | i ∈ I}
which does not intersect with A and has the same cardinality as A. Let hĀi be a free
group with basis Ā. We denote the operation in this group by ◦. Any element of hĀi can
be uniquely presented by a reduced word of the form
                                             ◦(k )      ◦(k )            ◦(k )
                                     w = āi1 1 ◦ āi2 2 ◦ . . . ◦ āis s ,

where āij ∈ Ā, kij ∈ Z \ {0}. Deﬁne a map β̄ : hĀi → G by the rule

                       β̄(w) = β(ai1 )k1 β(ai2 )k2 . . . β(ais )ks = uki11 uki22 . . . ukiss .

It is easy to see that this map is a homomorphism of hĀi to hUi.
    Deﬁne a map π : hĀi → G by the formula

   π(w) = (ai1 β(ai1 ))k1 (ai2 β(ai2 ))k2 . . . (ais β(ais ))ks β(ais )−ks β(ais−1 )−ks−1 . . . β(ai1 )−k1 .

The following lemma clariﬁes the connection between these two maps.

                                                        14
Lemma 7.3. Let w, w ′ ∈ hĀi, then
  a) π(w ◦(−1) ) = β̄(w)−1π(w)−1 β̄(w),
  b) π(w ◦ w ′ ) = π(w)β̄(w)π(w ′)β̄(w)−1,
  c) π((w ′)◦(−1) ◦ w ◦ w ′ ) = β̄(w ′)−1 π(w ′)−1 π(w)β̄(w)π(w ′)β̄(w)−1 β̄(w ′).

Proof. a) For the word
                                              ◦(k )         ◦(k )                 ◦(k )
                                      w = āi1 1 ◦ āi2 2 ◦ . . . ◦ āis s
its inverse equals
                                             ◦(−ks )         ◦(−k     )               ◦(−k1 )
                               w ◦(−1) = āis            ◦ āis−1 s−1 ◦ . . . ◦ āi1            ,
and

π(w ◦(−1) )=(ais β(ais ))−ks (ais−1 β(ais−1 ))−ks−1 . . . (ai1 β(ai1 ))−k1 β(ai1 )k1 β(ai2 )k2 . . . β(ais )ks .

Hence,
                  π(w ◦(−1) ) = β(ais )−ks . . . β(ai1 )−k1 π(w)−1β(ai1 )k1 . . . β(ais )ks .
   b) Given a word
                                                 ◦(l )      ◦(l )             ◦(l )
                                      w ′ = āj1 1 ◦ āj2 2 ◦ . . . ◦ ājt t ,
we compute
                                         ◦(k )                ◦(k )       ◦(l )             ◦(l )
                           w ◦ w ′ = āi1 1 ◦ . . . ◦ āis s ◦ āj1 1 ◦ . . . ◦ ājt t
and

  π(w ◦ w ′ ) = (ai1 β(ai1 ))k1 . . . (ais β(ais ))ks · (aj1 β(aj1 ))l1 . . . (ajt β(ajt ))lt
                                                          · β(ajl )−lt . . . β(aj1 )−l1 · β(ais )−ks . . . β(ai1 )−k1 .

Hence,

π(w◦w ′) = π(w)β(ai1 )k1 . . . β(ais )ks π(w ′)·β(ais )−ks . . . β(ai1 )−k1 = π(w)β̄(w)π(w ′)β̄(w)−1.

   c) Take the product (w ′ )◦(−1) ◦ w ◦ w ′ and ﬁnd

  π((w ′)◦(−1) ◦ w ◦ w ′ ) = β(ajl )−lt . . . β(aj1 )−l1 (π(w ′)−1 π(w)β(ai1 )k1 . . . β(ais )ks π(w ′)
                              · β(ais )−ks . . . β(ai1 )−k1 )β(aj1 )l1 . . . β(ajt )lt
                                               = β̄(w ′ )−1 π(w ′)−1 π(w)β̄(w)π(w ′)β̄(w)−1β̄(w ′ ).

   Let R = {w ∈ hĀi | π(w) = e}. Then from the previous lemma it follows

Lemma 7.4. The set R is a subgroup of hĀi. Suppose that β̄ satisﬁes the following
implication
                        π(w) = π(w ′) ⇒ β̄(w) = β̄(w ′),                      (7.1)
in particular, ker(π) ⊆ ker(β̄), then R is normal in hĀi.

Lemma 7.5. Suppose that for some elements w, w ′ ∈ hĀi such that π(w) = π(w ′ ), we
have β̄(w) 6= β̄(w ′ ), then β has no an extension to an RB-operator on G.

                                                            15
Proof. Suppose that B is an extension of β to an RB-operator B on G and
                        ◦(k )      ◦(k )          ◦(k )                ◦(l )     ◦(l )           ◦(l )
                w = āi1 1 ◦ āi2 2 ◦ . . . ◦ āis s ,         w ′ = āj1 1 ◦ āj2 2 ◦ . . . ◦ ājt t .

Consider two elements in GB :
                        ◦(k )      ◦(k )          ◦(k )                ◦(l )    ◦(l )            ◦(l )
                 u = ai1 1 ◦ ai2 2 ◦ . . . ◦ ais s ,           u′ = aj1 1 ◦ aj2 2 ◦ . . . ◦ ajt t .

   Then

         B(u) = β(ai1 )k1 . . . β(ais )ks = β̄(w) 6= β̄(w ′) = β(aj1 )l1 . . . β(ajt )lt = B(u′).

On the other hand,
                                  B(u) = B(π(w)) = B(π(w ′)) = B(u′ ),
a contradiction.
    If R = ker(π) is a normal subgroup of hĀi, then we can deﬁne a group Ḡβ = hĀi/R.
Denote by [w] the element of Ḡβ that is presented by the word w. The product in Ḡβ
is deﬁned by the rule [w] ◦ [w ′ ] = [w ◦ w ′ ]. Then Ḡβ is generated by [ai ], i ∈ I, and is
deﬁned by the relations [w] = [w ′ ] for all words
                        ◦(k )       ◦(k )         ◦(k )                 ◦(l )    ◦(l )            ◦(l )
                w = āi1 1 ◦ āi2 2 ◦ . . . ◦ āis s ,         w ′ = āj1 1 ◦ āj2 2 ◦ . . . ◦ ājt t

such that π(w) = π(w ′ ), i. e., the following relation holds in G:

  (ai1 β(ai1 ))k1 (ai2 β(ai2 ))k2 . . . (ais β(ais ))ks β(ais )−ks β(ais−1 )−ks−1 . . . β(ai1 )−k1
              = (aj1 β(aj1 ))l1 (aj2 β(aj2 ))l2 . . . (ajt β(ajt ))lt β(ajl )−lt β(ajt−1 )−lt−1 . . . β(aj1 )−l1 .

    If condition (7.1) is satisﬁed, then the homomorphism β̄ : hĀi → hUi ≤ G induces
the homomorphism Ḡβ → hUi, which we denote by the same symbol β̄. Also, the map
π : hĀi → G induces the map Ḡβ → G, which we denote by π̄. It is easy to see that
Im (π) = Im (π̄).
    In the following example we apply Lemma 7.5.
Example 7.6. Let

                                G = s1 , s2 | s21 = s22 = e, s1 s2 s1 = s2 s1 s2

be the symmetric group S3 on 3 symbols.
   a) If we take the map β : {s1 , s2 } → {s1 , s2 } such that s1 7→ s1 , s2 7→ s2 , then it has
an extension to the RB-operator B−1 (g) = g −1 on S3 . Let us ﬁnd the group Gβ . Let hĀi
be a free group with basis Ā = {t1 , t2 }. We have a map π : hĀi → G that is deﬁned by
the formula
                   ◦(k )  ◦(l )          ◦(k )  ◦(l ) 
                π t1 1 ◦ t2 1 ◦ . . . ◦ t1 s ◦ t2 s = s−l  s −ks
                                                         2 s1    . . . s−l1 −k1
                                                                        2 s1 .

In this case R = {w ∈ hĀi | π(w) = e} is normal in hĀi and the product in Gβ is opposite
to the product in G.

                                                          16
   b) Note that the group S3 can be also generated by the elements τ1 = s1 , τ2 = s2 ,
and τ3 = s1 s2 s1 . Put

                                β(τ1 ) = τ1 ,      β(τ2 ) = τ2 ,      β(τ3 ) = τ2 τ1

and take hĀi be a free group with basis Ā = {t1 , t2 , t3 }. Then

     π(t1 ◦ t1 ) = π(t2 ◦ t2 ) = π(t3 ◦ t1 ) = e,           π(t1 ◦ t2 ◦ t1 ) = π(t2 ◦ t1 ◦ t2 ) = τ1 τ2 τ1 ,
   π(t1 ◦ t2 ) = π(t2 ◦ t3 ) = π(t3 ◦ t3 ) = τ2 τ1 ,        π(t2 ◦ t1 ) = π(t3 ◦ t2 ) = π(t1 ◦ t3 ) = τ1 τ2 .

Hence, π(hĀi) = S3 .
   On the other hand,
                                      e = β̄(t1 ◦ t1 ) 6= β̄(t3 ◦ t1 ) = t2 .
It means that the condition of Lemma 7.5 does not hold and we can not extend the map β
to a Rota—Baxter operator on S3 .
    Now we can formulate the main result of the present section.
Theorem 7.7. Let G = hAi be a group generated by a set A = {ai | i ∈ I}. Suppose that
U = {ui }i∈I is a subset of G with the same cardinality as A and β : A → U, β(ai ) = ui ,
i ∈ I. If condition (7.1) is satisﬁed and the map π̄ : Ḡβ → G is bijective, then β can be
extended to an RB-operator on G and GB is isomorphic to Ḡβ .
Proof. Construct the RB-operator B on G. Let g ∈ G. Since π̄ is invertible on G, there
exists a unique element ḡ ∈ Ḡβ such that π̄(ḡ) = g. Suppose that ḡ = [w], where
                                                ◦(k )    ◦(k )             ◦(k )
                                      w = āi1 1 ◦ āi2 2 ◦ . . . ◦ āis s

is a word in the free group hĀi. Then we put

                        B(g) = B(π̄(ḡ)) = B(π(w)) = β̄(w) = uki11 uki22 . . . ukiss .

By condition (7.1) this map is deﬁned on [w] and does not depend on the choice of w.
   Let us prove that B is an RB-operator on G. For g ′ ∈ G there exists a word
                                                 ◦(l )   ◦(l )             ◦(l )
                                       w ′ = āj1 1 ◦ āj2 2 ◦ . . . ◦ ājt t

such that π(w ′) = π̄([w ′ ]) = g ′ . Then B(g ′ ) = ulj11 ulj22 . . . uljtt .
   On the other hand, by Lemma 7.3b

                                   π(w ◦ w ′ ) = π(w)β̄(w)π(w ′)β̄(w)−1

and we have

  B(gB(g)g ′B(g)−1) = B(π(w ◦ w ′ )) = β̄(w ◦ w ′ ) = β̄(w)β̄(w ′ )
                                                          = uki11 uki22 . . . ukiss · ulj11 ulj22 . . . uljtt = B(g)B(g ′).

Hence, B is indeed an RB-operator on G.

                                                         17
   The next proposition shows that the condition (7.1) is not suﬃcient for existence of
an RB-operator extending given map β.
Proposition 7.8. Consider the symmetric group S3 . Then
   a) the map β : s1 7→ s1 , s2 7→ e deﬁnes the group Ḡβ and this group is isomorphic to
Z2 × Z2 .
   b) There is no an RB-operator on S3 extending β.
Proof. a) Take a free group ht1 , t2 i. Then we can ﬁnd

                  π(t1 ◦ t1 ) = π(t2 ◦ t2 ) = e,        π(t1 ◦ t2 ) = π(t2 ◦ t1 ) = s2 s1 .

From equalities

                   β̄(t1 ◦ t1 ) = β̄(t2 ◦ t2 ) = e,        β̄(t1 ◦ t2 ) = β̄(t2 ◦ t1 ) = s1

it follows that (7.1) holds and we can deﬁne

       Ḡβ = h[t1 ], [t2 ] | [t1 ] ◦ [t1 ] = [t2 ] ◦ [t2 ] = e, [t1 ] ◦ [t2 ] = [t2 ] ◦ [t1 ]i ∼
                                                                                               = Z2 × Z2 .

Hence, the map β does not deﬁne a group operation on the set S3 .
   b) Suppose that such RB-operator B exists. Since B(s2 ) = e, then by Lemma 2.7

                                 B(s1 s2 ) = B(s2 s1 s2 ) = B(s1 s2 s1 ).

We arrive at a contradiction by the following equalities,

      s1 B(s1 s2 ) = B(s1 )B(s1 s2 ) = B(s1 · s1 · s1 s2 · s1 ) = B(s1 s2 s1 ) = B(s1 s2 ).

   Now we consider RB-operators on free non-abelian groups. In this case we do not
need to deﬁne groups hĀi and Ḡβ . We can deﬁne a new operation ◦ directly on the free
group.
   The following proposition shows that in some cases we can reconstruct RB-operators
by its values on a basis of a free group.
Proposition 7.9. Let F be a free group with a basis A = {ai }i∈I . Then
   a) the map β : ai 7→ e for all i ∈ I has the unique extension to an RB-operator. This
operator is the trivial one, B0 (g) = e, g ∈ F .
   b) the map β : ai 7→ a−1 i  for all i ∈ I has the unique extension to an RB-operator.
This operator is B−1 (g) = g −1 , g ∈ F .
Proof. a) Suppose that B is an extension of β to an RB-operator on F . Below we use
                                                                 ◦(k)
the notation of the operation ◦ in sense of (3.1). In this case ai    = aki , and hence
    ◦(k)
B(ai ) = e for all i ∈ I, k ∈ Z. If
                                            ◦(k )     ◦(k )           ◦(k )
                                    w = ai1 1 ◦ ai2 2 ◦ . . . ◦ ais s ,

where aij ∈ A, kij ∈ Z, is an arbitrary word, then
                                    ◦(k )  ◦(k )    ◦(k ) 
                      B(w) = B ai1 1 B ai2 2 . . . B ais s = e.

                                                      18
Let us show that in this case GB is also generated by A. It follows from the equality
          ◦(k )     ◦(k )           ◦(k )
  w = ai1 1 ◦ ai2 2 ◦ . . . ◦ ais s
      = (ai1 B(ai1 ))k1 (ai2 B(ai2 ))k2 . . . (ais B(ais ))ks B(ais )−ks B(ais−1 )−ks−1 . . . B(ai1 )−k1
                                                                                                  = aki11 aki22 . . . akiss .
    b) The proof is similar.
Question 7.10. Find Rota—Baxter operators on free non-abelian groups. In particular,
is it true that any map β deﬁned on a basis of a free group can be extended to an
RB-operator on this group?
   The following example shows that the values of β on the generators of Fn do not
deﬁne values of β on all elements of Fn .
Example 7.11. Let F2 = ha, bi be the free group of rank 2. Put β(a) = a, β(b) = e.
By Proposition 5.9, there exists an RB-operator on F2 which is extension of the map β.
This operator is the homomorphism B : F2 → hai that is deﬁned on the generators as
follows, B(a) = β(a) = a, B(b) = β(b) = e. Let us denote the product in F2 as · and the
product in (F2 )B as ◦. We try do deﬁne the operation ◦ on F2 applying only the map β.
We have
                             a◦(k) = ak ,      β(a◦(k) ) = β(a)k = ak ,           k ∈ Z,
                                b◦(l) = bl ,    β(b◦(l) ) = β(b)l = e,          l ∈ Z.
For words of syllable length two we have
                       a◦(k) ◦ b◦(l) = a2k bl a−k ,      b◦(l) ◦ a◦(k) = bl ak ,      k, l ∈ Z.
By Proposition 3.4 for word of an arbitrary length we have
                                                                                                                   P

   Hence, S is not equal to F2 . In particular, ab does not lie in S.
   Let us add a new generator ab to the set {a, b} and put
                                     β1 (a) = β1 (ab) = a,              β1 (b) = e.

                                                          19
Question 7.12. Is it true that the group (F2 )B from this example is not ﬁnitely gener-
ated?

   In Example 7.11 we have deﬁned β on the group h{a, b}, ◦i that is a subset of F2 . We
have seen that β has a non-trivial kernel and its image is not equal to F2 .

Question 7.13. Is there an RB-group (G, B) such that B is a surjective map with
a non-trivial kernel?


8    Extensions of RB-groups
    If (G, B) is an RB-group, then an RB-group (H, BH ) is called an RB-subgroup of
(G, B), if H is a subgroup of G and BH is the restriction of B to H. We can deﬁne
a short exact sequence of RB-groups

                        1 → (H, BH ) → (G, B) → (L, BL ) → 1,                      (8.1)

where (H, BH ) is an RB-subgroup of (G, B) and there is an epimorphism of RB-groups
(G, B) → (L, BL ) such that BL is induced by B. We say that (G, B) is an extension of
(H, BH ) by (L, BL ).
   As in the case of groups we can formulate

Question 8.1. Let (H, BH ) and (L, HL ) be two RB-groups. Find all RB-groups (G, B)
for which there exists the short exact sequence (8.1)?

   By Proposition 6.1, such RB-groups (G, B) exist.
   Recall the construction of wreath product (see, for example, [16]). Let H and L be
groups, Fun(L, H) and fun(L, H) are Cartesian and direct sums of copies H indexed
by elements of L. It means that Fun(L, H) is the group of all functions L → H and
fun(L, H) is its subgroup of functions with a ﬁnite support. For f ∈ Fun(L, H), l ∈ L,
the function f l is deﬁned by the rule f l = f (lx), x ∈ L. The map
                         ˆl : Fun(L, H) → Fun(L, H),   f 7→ f l ,

is an automorphism of Fun(L, H), which sends fun(L, H) to itself, and the maps

                L → Aut(Fun(L, H)),      L → Aut(fun(L, H)),        l 7→ ˆl,

are isomorphic embeddings. The Cartesian wreath product H¯≀L = L · Fun(L, H) is
a group with multiplication
                                                     ′
                              lf · l′ f ′ = ll′ · f l f ′ .
The direct wreath product is the group H ≀ L = L · fun(L, H).
   It is natural to formulate

Question 8.2. Let G = H ≀ L be a direct wreath product or G = H¯≀L be a Cartesian
wreath product of H and L. What RB-operators can be deﬁned on G?


                                          20
    Particular answer on this question gives
Proposition 8.3. Let G be a Cartesian or direct wreath product of groups H and L.
Then
   a) the map B(lf ) = f −1 deﬁnes an RB-operator on G;
   b) if L is abelian and ϕ is any endomorphism of L, then the map B(lf ) = lϕ deﬁnes
an RB-operator on G;
   c) if action of L on Fun(L, H) (correspondingly, on fun(L, H)) is trivial and BL and
BH are RB-operators on L and on Fun(L, H) (on fun(L, H) respectively), then the map
B(lf ) = BL (l)BH (f ) deﬁnes an RB-operator on G.
Proof. a) Since G has exact factorization G = L · Fun(L, H) or G = L · fun(L, H), then
the result follows from Example 4.1.
   b) Follows from Proposition 5.1b.
   c) Follows from Proposition 6.1.
   Non-trivial examples of RB-operators on Fun(L, H) and on fun(L, H) can be found
by Theorem 6.3.
   It is well-known that any extension of a group H by a group L can be embedded into
the Cartesian wreath product H¯≀L, it is the Frobenius embedding.
   For extensions of RB-groups we can formulate
Question 8.4. Is it true that any RB-extension of (H, BH ) by (L, BL ) can be embedded
into an RB-group (H¯≀L, B) for some an RB-operator B on H¯≀L?
    By analogy with extension and lifting problems for automorphism groups of exten-
sions, we can formulate
Question 8.5. Suppose that
                                 1→H→G→L→1
is a short exact sequence of groups.
    a) Extension problem. Let (H, BH ) be an RB-group. Does there exist an RB-group
(G, B) such that (H, BH ) is its RB-subgroup?
    b) Lifting problem. Let (L, BL ) be an RB-group. Do there exist an RB-group (G, B)
and an epimorphism (G, B) → (L, BL ) such that BL is induced by B?


9     Connection with associated Lie ring
   The main motivation of the authors L. Guo et al. [14] to introduce Rota—Baxter
operators on groups was the connection with Rota—Baxter operators on Lie algebras,
when the initial group is Lie one. Let us consider another known construction of Lie ring
by a given (not necessary Lie) group.
   Let G be a group, consider its lower central series Gi , i = 1, 2, L
                                                                      . . ., where G1 = G
and Gi+1 = [G, Gi ]. The associated graded abelian group L(G) = n≥1 Gn /Gn+1 has
the structure of Lie ring under the product [xGi+1 , yGj+1] = [x, y]Gi+j+1, where [x, y] is
usual commutator.

                                            21
Proposition 9.1. Let G be a group and let B be a Rota—Baxter operator on G such that
B(Gn ) ⊂ Gn for all n ≥ 1. Then R deﬁned as R(xGi+1 ) = B(x)Gi+1 is a Rota—Baxter
operator of weight 1 on the Lie ring L(G).

Proof. Given h ∈ Gi and g ∈ Gi+1 , it is easy to check by Lemma 2.5d that B(h)−1 B(hg) ∈
Gi+1 , so R is well-deﬁned. Let x ∈ Gi and y ∈ Gj . We have to state the equality

  [R(xGi+1 ), R(yGj+1)] = R([R(xGi+1 ), yGj+1] + [xGi+1 , R(yGj+1)] + [xGi+1 , yGj+1]),

which equals in terms of B to the following one,

     B(x)−1 B(y)−1 B(x)B(y)Gi+j+1 = B([B(x), y] + [x, B(y)] + [x, y])Gi+j+1.            (9.1)

Applying the commutator properties and the fact that Gi+j /Gi+j+1 is abelian, we may
rewrite the inner expression inside the brackets from the right-hand side of (9.1) modulo
Gi+j+1 as follows,

 [B(x), y] + [x, B(y)] + [x, y]
       = [B(x), y]B(y) + [x, B(y)]B(x) + [x, y]B(y)B(x) + [B(x), B(y)] + [B(y), B(x)]
      = [x, yB(y)]B(x) + [B(x), yB(y)] + [B(y), B(x)] = [xB(x), yB(y)] + [B(y), B(x)].

The formula (9.1) is a consequence of the equalities fulﬁlled in G

 B(y)B(x)B([xB(x), yB(y)] · [B(y), B(x)])
              = B(yB(y)xB(y)−1)B([xB(x), yB(y)] · [B(y), B(x)])
             = B yB(y)xB(y)−1B(y)B(x)(xB(x))−1 (yB(y))−1xB(x)yB(y)
                                                           
                     × B(y)−1 B(x)−1 B(y)B(x)B(x)−1 B(y)−1
           = B(yB(y)xB(x)B(x)−1 x−1 B(y)−1y −1 xB(x)yB(x)−1 B(y)B(y)−1)
                                  = B(yB(y)B(y)−1y −1xB(x)yB(x)−1 ) = B(x)B(y).

Example 9.2. Let G be a 2-step nilpotent group and B is an RB-operator on G deﬁned
as in Proposition 5.4. Then by Proposition 9.1 we get an RB-operator R : L(G) → L(G),
where L(G) = G/[G, G] ⊕ [G, G]. It is easy to verify that R = −id.


10     Rota—Baxter operators on ﬁnite simple groups
   Given a group G, an automorphism ψ of G is called ﬁxed-point-free, if ψ(g) = g
implies g = e. Let us state a group analogue of Proposition 2.21 from [6] proven for Lie
algebras (see also [4]).

Theorem 10.1. Let G be a ﬁnite non-abelian simple group. Let B be a Rota—Baxter
operator on G such that ker B = {e}. Then B(g) = g −1 .



                                            22
Proof. Since B is a homomorphism from GB to G with trivial kernel, we conclude that
GB ∼= G, and GB is also simple. Suppose that ker(B+ ) 6= GB , where B+ (g) = gB(g) is
a homomorphism from GB to G. By simplicity of GB , we obtain that ker B+ = {e}. So,
we have an automorphism ϕ = B −1 B+ of the simple group GB . Note that ϕ is a ﬁxed-
point-free. Indeed, g = ϕ(g) = B −1 (gB(g)) would imply the equality B(g) = gB(g), i. e.,
g = e. By [19], a ﬁnite group admitting a ﬁxed-point-free automorphism is solvable. We
have a contradiction.
Corollary 10.2. Let G be a ﬁnite group and let B be an RB-operator on G. If the
group GB is non-abelian simple, then B is elementary and G ∼
                                                           = GB .
Proof. Since ker B is a normal subgroup of GB and GB is simple, we have two cases:
either ker B = G or ker B = {e}. If ker B = G, then B is elementary and G ∼
                                                                          = GB . If
                     ∼
ker B = {e}, then G = GB by Theorem 10.1.
Corollary 10.3. Let G be a ﬁnite non-abelian simple group. If G is not factorizable,
then G is RB-elementary.
Proof. Let B be a nonelementary Rota—Baxter operator on such a group G. By Theo-
rem 10.1 we have a proper factorization (3.3), it is a contradiction.
   List of ﬁnite simple non-factorizable groups is presented in [17, Table 4.1]. It includes
some ﬁnite groups of Lie type (classical and exceptional) and 15 sporadic groups. We are
going to describe all Rota—Baxter operators on all sporadic groups.

                    Table: exact factorizations of sporadic groups [8]
                         G        A                  B
                       M11       M10                 Z11
                                M9 .2             Z11 ⋊ Z5
                       M12       M11         A4 , D12 , Z6 × Z2
                                M9 .2             PSL2 (11)
                       M23       M22                 Z23
                              Z23 ⋊ Z11      PΣL3 (4), 24 ⋊ A7
                       M24       M23      A4 × Z2 , D24 , D8 ⋊ Z3
                                 M23                 S4
                                 M23                 B24
                              PSL2 (23)      PΣL3 (4), 24 ⋊ A7

Theorem 10.4. Let G be a sporadic simple group. If G = M22 or G is not a Mathieu
group, then G has only elementary RB-operators. If G ∈ {M11 , M12 , M23 , M24 }, then all
RB-operators on G are splitting (see Table).
Proof. Our main tool in the proof is the list of all factorizations of sporadic groups [8].
Suppose that B is a nonelementary RB-operator on G. Thus, ker B 6= {e} and ker(B+ ) 6=
{e} by Corollary 10.3. We have a factorization (3.3). Suppose that one of the factors
in (3.3) is simple. We may assume that Im (B) is simple, otherwise we consider B    e and
     e Since ker B+ is a normal subgroup of Im (B), we conclude that ker B+ = Im (B).
Im (B).

                                            23
By (3.2), Im B+ = ker B. The last equality due to Proposition 4.2 implies that B is
splitting.
    Suppose initially that a factorization (3.3) is exact. Since |G| = | ker B| · |Im B|, we
again get the equality ker B+ = Im (B), and so B is splitting.
    Now, we look through all factorizations of sporadic groups. In Tables 1 and 2 [8] we
have only one non-exact factorization with both non-simple factors, it is

                            He = (Sp(4, 4).2) · (72 ⋊ SL2 (7)).

Let Im (B) = Sp(4, 4).2 and Im (B+ ) = 72 ⋊SL2 (7), then | ker B| = |He|/|Im (B)| = 2058.
Since |Im (B+ )| = 8 · 2058, we get by (3.2) that ker(B+ ) is a subgroup of Im (B) of
index 8. Analyzing maximal subgroups of Sp(4, 4) [7], we conclude that this case for
a Rota—Baxter operator B is not possible.
